lines: You brought me back without needing the worst of it. Restraint is a weapon too.
Home again, whole enough to thank you properly. That matters.
We came back with the village still ahead of us. I will count that as good work.
The forge sounded better than music when we reached the gate.
I carried less steel than usual and still felt prepared.
Good judgment brought us home more surely than a sharp blade could.
I watched every turn so I could find the route again.
The road nearly outlasted our food, but not our sense.
Thanks for sharing the last of the supplies without making a speech.
I kept pace on the rough ground because you did not rush me.
Seeing the village roofs again loosened every muscle in my shoulders.
The bell at the end of the road told me we had made it.
Next time I bring more food and fewer weapons.
No one drew steel. That is the best report I can give.
A safe return is worth more than a glorious story.
I trusted your route, and this time that trust came home intact.
The first thing I did was put the weapon away and breathe.
We left together and returned together. Good work.
I learned when to carry a blade and when to trust the road.
Give me one quiet shift at the forge and I may be ready to go again.
I came back marked. Next time, keep the edge between us and danger.
I made it home, but the road took more from me than it should have.
Next time, let us return with fewer marks and better choices.
Every step pulled at the wound before we reached the gate.
I hated slowing the group, but I could not hide it forever.
The first safe doorway was the finest thing I saw all day.
Blood dried on the road before I could clean the blade.
I should carry bandages beside the whetstone from now on.
The forge felt impossibly far away while we were walking home.
Neighbors took my weight at the gate. I will remember that.
Survival matters more than keeping a blade unmarked.
I made the mistake of treating pain like a test of pride.
Next time I stop and bind the wound before it gets worse.
A weapon cannot help much when the hand holding it is shaking.
I came home with the steel and nearly left my strength behind.
The road taught my ribs a lesson the forge never could.
I was not brave. I was stubborn enough to keep walking.
Give me time to heal before you ask me to call that trip worthwhile.
I know exactly which piece of gear failed me. It will not fail twice.
We reached home. Today, that is enough victory.
I respect sharp steel. I do not respect turning it on someone who followed you.
Following you was trust. What happened after was something else.
A guide who strikes from close by leaves the longest mark.
I keep my weapon between us now. You taught me that.
The bruise faded faster than the suspicion did.
I watched the road while the real danger walked beside me.
Do not ask me to admire your aim. There was nothing honorable in it.
The walk home was quiet because trust had already said its last word.
I can repair chipped steel. I cannot repair this for you.
You knew my guard was down. That makes it worse.
I will hear you out, but I will not turn my back.
A clean apology would help more than another excuse.
I followed your lead once. You will have to earn that privilege again.
The forge felt safer than the road after what you did.
I have handled rough weapons with better discipline than yours.
Next time, I choose the route and keep you in sight.
You turned a simple journey into a lesson I did not need.
The worst part was realizing the attack came from someone I trusted.
I made it home, but I left my faith in you on that road.
If there is a next time, honesty comes before the first step.
A boat is not armor, but it kept danger at a decent distance.
The boat did its part. I am still deciding whether the rest of the plan did.
Water carried us home, which is more than I expected from that journey.
I should have left the heavy blade at the forge.
The current handled our route like it had made the plan itself.
I checked the sheath three times and the hull far more than that.
A sharp edge is little comfort when the water is deeper than you are tall.
I was glad to hear the grindstone again when we returned.
Next time we inspect the boat before either of us steps inside.
There was barely room for two people and no room for bad judgment.
I kept still because rocking the boat solved nothing.
The village looked better with every stroke toward shore.
My hands wanted a hammer, a rail, or anything that did not move.
I trust solid ground more than I did before that trip.
The hull held, the sheath stayed shut, and we came home. Good enough.
I could not fight the current, so I learned to respect it.
That knocking under the boat sounded worse than a cracked blade.
I will bring less steel and more dry food next time.
Stepping onto land felt like setting down a weapon after a long watch.
I am not eager to repeat the trip, but I know how to prepare now.
